title: Multiple Sort Keys
description: Order SQL rows by multiple columns with separate ASC and DESC directions; trace left-to-right priorities and use a final key to resolve ties.
notes:
## Several keys express a priority order

A multi-key [ORDER BY](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/order-by) compares result rows using a sequence of priorities. A campus catalogue can list categories alphabetically, then show expensive products first within each category. The second key does not compete equally with the first. It is consulted only when the earlier key does not distinguish the rows. That priority structure is the essential meaning of a multi-key order.

State the requirement in that same hierarchy: category first, price within category, identity within any remaining tie. This is often easier to review than a flat list of desired properties. If the business instead wants the most expensive product overall first, price must become the earlier key. Reordering the terms changes the ranking contract rather than merely changing formatting.

## Compare rows at their first differing key

To compare two rows, inspect the first sort expression. If their values differ under its comparison rules, that expression decides their order. Only if those values tie do you inspect the next expression. Continue until a key distinguishes the rows or all stated keys tie. This is often called lexicographic ordering, even when some keys are numeric rather than textual.

Consider a Books product priced at three hundred and an Electronics product priced at eighty thousand. Under category-first order, the Books row can come first regardless of its lower price. The price key becomes relevant only within equal categories. A sample containing several categories with very different prices makes this priority visible and exposes a query that accidentally sorts globally by price.

```sql
SELECT id, name, category, price
FROM products
ORDER BY category ASC, price DESC, id ASC;
```

## Each key owns its direction

A multi-key sort can mix ascending and descending directions. Category ascending and price descending is a valid combination because the directions apply to different comparison priorities. A DESC attached to price does not reverse category ordering or the direction of a later identity key. Write directions explicitly when the mixture is central to the feature.

The omitted direction on an ordinary term defaults to ascending. Relying on that default is legal, but a clear maintained query can spell out every direction to reduce misreading. The purpose is communicative consistency rather than a universal performance change. A query's actual access strategy depends on the complete expression, available indexes and data distribution.

## Complete ties remain unspecified until resolved

Two rows can share both category and price. With only those keys, their relative order is not fully specified. It is not automatically alphabetical by name, insertion order or primary-key order. Add another term when the consumer needs deterministic ordering. A unique id is a suitable final tie breaker when the result contains one row per product.

The retained intermediate exercise preserves its category and price priorities and states ascending id for otherwise equal rows. Earlier source samples contain no such ties, so that final key preserves their visible order while making a previously unspecified case explicit. New tie fixtures show why the extension matters. Keep the source identity and setup intact rather than replace the exercise to avoid explaining ties.

## A label can itself have equivalent comparisons

Text keys use their applicable collation. Two category spellings may compare equal under case-insensitive rules even if their displayed strings differ. The next key can then influence their relative positions. A reader expecting strict byte distinctions may find the result surprising unless the comparison contract is stated. Do not assume that visual spelling alone defines every sort boundary.

A unique numeric identity at the end can resolve remaining row ties even when earlier labels compare equivalently. It does not force those labels into a different collation order. If the product requires a specific language-aware or exact-case category presentation, define that text comparison explicitly and test representative labels rather than treat id as a substitute for the intended primary sort semantics.

## Result grain determines a useful final key

A product table's [primary key](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/primary-key) distinguishes its base rows, but a join can repeat a product once per matching tag or checkout. In that result, product id alone may still leave ties. Include the relevant relationship or event identity if the report intentionally returns several rows per product. Otherwise revise the query to express the desired one-row-per-product grain before ordering.

Do not add DISTINCT casually to hide those repeated rows. It can change the report meaning or conceal a missing join condition. Understand whether multiplicity is intended, then choose projection and ordering together. A deterministic sequence of the wrong row population is still an incorrect query, just as a correct population with unspecified ties can still violate an export contract.

## Custom priority keys need an explicit mapping

A report may order urgent requests before normal requests regardless of their text labels. A CASE expression can map those statuses to priority numbers, followed by timestamp and identity keys. Define what happens to unknown or newly added statuses. A mapping that assigns every unexpected state the highest priority can change the workflow when new data appears.

Computed priorities are ordinary ordering expressions rather than permission checks. The report may rank a row first without granting the caller authority to act on it. Validate privileged transitions at the trusted boundary and keep the ranking policy documented in the query contract. Sorting an interface is not a substitute for enforcing which records that interface is allowed to retrieve.

## Missing values form another ordering dimension

A nullable price or timestamp can have an engine-specific default placement. If the feature needs missing values last while known prices descend, make missingness a separate key before the value. Then apply a unique identity after the known-value priority. Each term has one role: present versus absent grouping, value ranking and final deterministic tie resolution.

Replacing NULL with a large numeric sentinel can merge unknown data with a legitimate extreme value. A Boolean missingness key avoids changing the source fact. For cross-engine code, use the supported syntax and equivalent tested rules for each engine rather than assume default NULL placement is portable. Sorting policy should be visible even when the current sample happens to contain no missing values.

## Pagination depends on the full key tuple

A page boundary defined only by price is incomplete when several rows share that price. Continuation needs the same complete ordering tuple that determines position, including directions and any missingness policy. If the display order is category, descending price and ascending id, a cursor or comparison rule based solely on id does not describe the same sequence.

Stable keys do not freeze changing data between requests. Inserts, removals and updates can move items relative to a page boundary. Decide whether the feature needs a snapshot, a best-effort live list or a durable export. The ordering tuple supports that design but does not by itself provide its visibility or consistency guarantees. Test ties around boundaries when implementing pagination separately.

## Index alignment is evidence to inspect

An index can sometimes help satisfy an ordering when its key layout and the query's restrictions fit the required priorities and directions. That is not a guarantee for every multi-key expression. Filtering, computed terms, join shape and the chosen plan can change whether additional sorting is needed. Establish the correct sequence first, then inspect a representative plan if performance matters.

Avoid reordering keys merely to match an available index unless the requirement permits the changed ranking. Category-first and price-first lists are different products even if one happens to be cheaper to compute. An optimization must preserve the sequence contract, including tie order and NULL placement, rather than return an approximately similar sample that becomes wrong on more varied data.

## Verify priority changes with contrasting rows

The beginner exercise sorts inspection requests by rating descending, then cost ascending, then identity. It includes a lower-rated cheap request to show that price cannot outrank rating. The retained product exercise sorts category first and price second, with an explicit final identity tie breaker. Both provide alternative fixtures with complete and partial ties.

Check each adjacent pair in the expected output by identifying the first key that distinguishes it. If a cheaper row appears later, explain which higher-priority key decided the order. This reasoning exposes swapped keys, wrongly shared directions and omitted ties. A clear multi-key query makes every sequence decision traceable to the stated priority list instead of accidental source order.

references.title: MySQL 8.4 ORDER BY expressions and directions

questions.question_text: In ORDER BY category,price, what is price used for?
options: Sorting every row globally before category
Filtering expensive rows
Breaking ties on the earlier category key
Removing duplicate categories
questions.explanation: Keys have left-to-right priority.

questions.question_text: Does swapping category and price generally preserve sequence?
options: Yes, ordering keys are commutative
No, it changes the primary ranking priority
Only if both are numbers
Always if there are two keys
questions.explanation: Some samples may coincide, but the contracts differ.

questions.question_text: Can one key ascend while the next descends?
options: No, one direction applies to the entire list
Yes
Only for the final key
Only in a stored procedure
questions.explanation: Each term owns its direction.

questions.question_text: What does category ASC,price DESC do?
options: Order globally by high price
Order categories first, then high prices within equal categories
Reverse all category labels
Choose only one product per category
questions.explanation: The second term does not override the first.

questions.question_text: What if all stated sort keys tie?
options: Names always sort automatically
Relative order is unspecified without another distinguishing key
Insertion order is guaranteed
The query errors
questions.explanation: A final key can complete the contract.

questions.question_text: Does multi-key ORDER BY stop at two terms?
options: Yes, exactly two terms
Only one term is ever legal
No, use the needed supported key list
Only WHERE columns can be keys
questions.explanation: Avoid claiming an unlimited count across every implementation limit.

questions.question_text: Which priority gives highest rating first and cheapest within equal ratings?
options: cost ASC,rating DESC
rating DESC,cost ASC
rating ASC,cost DESC
cost DESC,rating ASC
questions.explanation: Rating is the primary comparison.

questions.question_text: How should category, best rating, then name be ordered?
options: category ASC,rating DESC,name ASC
name ASC,rating DESC,category ASC
rating DESC,name ASC,category DESC
category DESC,rating ASC,name DESC
questions.explanation: The key sequence follows the report hierarchy.

questions.question_text: What decides two rows when their categories differ?
options: The category key alone at that priority
The lower price automatically
The later id automatically
All keys vote equally
questions.explanation: Later terms are consulted only after earlier ties.

questions.question_text: Why add id after category and price?
options: To make price the primary key
To distinguish remaining ties when id is unique in the result
To remove categories
To change stored identities
questions.explanation: The extra term completes the sequence.

questions.question_text: Does price DESC make a following id term descending too?
options: Yes
No, its omitted direction defaults ascending
Only when prices tie
Only for text ids
questions.explanation: Directions do not propagate across commas.

questions.question_text: Why can a text category tie despite visibly different spelling?
options: Every string is byte-distinct under all collations
Category has no type
The applicable collation can compare the strings equivalently
ORDER BY ignores text
questions.explanation: Comparison semantics define ties.

questions.question_text: When can product id fail to resolve a joined result completely?
options: Whenever an index exists
Whenever price is positive
Whenever category is text
When the join intentionally returns several rows for that product
questions.explanation: The tie key must match result grain.

questions.question_text: Why not use DISTINCT automatically to fix join fanout?
options: It can change meaning or conceal a missing relationship condition
It always preserves every event
It is required by ORDER BY
It creates a primary key
questions.explanation: Resolve the population contract before ordering.

questions.question_text: What does a CASE priority key require for unexpected states?
options: A guaranteed highest rank for every new state
An explicit default or handling policy
Automatic authorization
A table deletion
questions.explanation: New states must not silently change the workflow.

questions.question_text: Why make NULL placement a separate key when needed?
options: It guarantees one fixed physical plan
It replaces every later key
It preserves missingness without inventing a numeric sentinel
It authorizes missing rows
questions.explanation: Missingness grouping and value ranking have separate roles.

questions.question_text: What tuple should a continuation design reflect?
options: Only whichever id is convenient
Only the first displayed text field
Only the row count
The complete ordering keys and their directions
questions.explanation: A cursor based on a different sequence can skip or repeat rows.

questions.question_text: Does a deterministic key tuple freeze changing data across requests?
options: No, consistency needs a separate visibility policy
Yes, for every user forever
Only when all keys ascend
Only when the tuple has three terms
questions.explanation: Stable ordering and stable data are different guarantees.

questions.question_text: Can keys be rearranged for index convenience without checking requirements?
options: Yes, every ordering is equivalent
No, that can change the product ranking
Only for large tables
Only when prices are integers
questions.explanation: Optimization must preserve the required sequence.

questions.question_text: How can one explain an adjacent pair in a sorted result?
options: Average every key together
Ignore all but the last term
Find the first key on which they differ
Assume insertion order
questions.explanation: That key and its direction justify the pair order.

coding_problems.title: Prioritize rating before cost
coding_problems.task: Return request_id,rating,cost sorted by rating descending, then cost ascending, then request_id ascending. Every fixture value is known. Preserve all requests.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE rated_requests(request_id INT PRIMARY KEY,rating INT NOT NULL,cost INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: A cheap low-rated request remains after higher-rated ones.
A complete rating-and-cost tie uses identity.
hints: Keep rating as the first key.
Specify a direction for every term.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT request_id,rating,cost FROM rated_requests ORDER BY rating DESC,cost ASC,request_id ASC;
coding_problems.explanation: Higher rating dominates lower cost. Cost decides only equal ratings, and identity decides the remaining complete tie.

coding_problems.title: Sort by Category, Then Price Descending
coding_problems.task: Return id,name,category,price for all products sorted by category ascending, then price descending within equal category. Resolve otherwise unspecified equal-category-and-price ties with id ascending. Preserve the original schema and sample.
coding_problems.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price) VALUES
(1, 'ProLaptop', 'Electronics', 85000),
(2, 'Desk Lamp', 'Home', 900),
(3, 'ProPhone', 'Electronics', 45000),
(4, 'Python Basics', 'Books', 350),
(5, 'Novel', 'Books', 220),
(6, 'Headphones', 'Electronics', 3000),
(7, 'Rug', 'Home', 4500);
coding_problems.expected:
id	name	category	price
4	Python Basics	Books	350
5	Novel	Books	220
1	ProLaptop	Electronics	85000
3	ProPhone	Electronics	45000
6	Headphones	Electronics	3000
7	Rug	Home	4500
2	Desk Lamp	Home	900
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: A costly Electronics item remains after Books under the category priority.
Equal category and price use ascending identity.
hints: Add id only after the original category and price priorities.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT id,name,category,price FROM products ORDER BY category ASC,price DESC,id ASC;
coding_problems.explanation: Category has the highest priority. Descending price applies within its ties, and ascending id specifies the previously unspecified complete tie without changing original sample order.

original_questions.question_text: In `ORDER BY category, price`, what role does `price` play?
options: It is the primary and only sort key
It sorts the whole table regardless of category
It only breaks ties among rows that already share the same category
It is ignored because only one ORDER BY key is allowed
original_questions.explanation: Secondary sort keys only apply within groups of equal values from the preceding key(s).

original_questions.question_text: Will `ORDER BY category, price` and `ORDER BY price, category` generally produce the same row order?
options: Yes, ORDER BY is commutative regardless of column order
No, because sort keys are applied in priority order left to right, so swapping them changes the result
Yes, but only if both columns are numeric
No, because SQL only allows one column in ORDER BY
original_questions.explanation: The leftmost column is the dominant sort key; swapping column order changes which one takes priority and produces a different overall order.

original_questions.question_text: Can different columns in a multi-key ORDER BY use different sort directions?
options: No, all columns must use the same direction
Yes, e.g. ORDER BY category ASC, rating DESC is valid
Only the first column can specify a direction
Only if using a stored procedure
original_questions.explanation: Each column in ORDER BY can independently specify ASC or DESC.

original_questions.question_text: Given rows with categories 'Electronics' and 'Home', and prices within each, what does `ORDER BY category, price DESC` do?
options: Sorts all rows by price descending, ignoring category
Groups rows alphabetically by category, then sorts each group's prices from highest to lowest
Sorts categories in reverse alphabetical order
Produces a syntax error because DESC must apply to all columns
original_questions.explanation: DESC applies only to the column it follows (price); category still sorts ascending (the default) as the primary key.

original_questions.question_text: If two products have the exact same category AND the exact same price, what determines their relative order under `ORDER BY category, price`?
options: They are guaranteed to appear in name-alphabetical order
Their order is unspecified unless an additional tiebreaker column is added
They are guaranteed to appear in insertion order
SQL raises an error for exact ties
original_questions.explanation: With no further tiebreaker column, rows tied on all specified sort keys have no guaranteed relative order.

original_questions.question_text: How many columns can appear in an ORDER BY clause?
options: Exactly one
At most two
Any number, separated by commas
Only as many as appear in the WHERE clause
original_questions.explanation: ORDER BY supports an arbitrary comma-separated list of sort expressions.

original_questions.question_text: You want the highest-rated product overall to appear first, and among equally-rated products, the cheapest first. Which ORDER BY achieves this?
options: ORDER BY price ASC, rating DESC
ORDER BY rating DESC, price ASC
ORDER BY rating, price
ORDER BY price, rating DESC
original_questions.explanation: Rating must be the primary (dominant) key in descending order, with price as the ascending tiebreaker.

original_questions.question_text: A report needs rows grouped by category (alphabetical), and within each category by rating (best first), and within equal ratings by name (alphabetical). Which clause is correct?
options: ORDER BY category, rating DESC, name
ORDER BY name, rating DESC, category
ORDER BY category DESC, rating, name
ORDER BY rating DESC, category, name
original_questions.explanation: The sort keys must be listed in priority order matching the requirement: category first, then rating descending, then name as final tiebreaker.
